beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about the multi-month trend investigation I built this week for the Mycroft Finance Investigator. Three months of verified finance data, compared. But the interesting engineering is not the comparison. It is that the engine tries fifteen separate times to refuse before it will compare anything at all.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the feature in the first breath
the ask types itself in, send button arms terracotta
running indicator: 'reading the build…'
three output lines land — three months, fifteen refusals, one blank field

props.command: Walk me through the trend investigation — the data, the refusals, and what it will not say.
output: Three verified months in: January, February and March.
Fifteen refusal paths run before any comparison is allowed.
And the “why did this happen” field ships deliberately blank.

beats.narration_text: Here is the rule the whole feature rests on, before any numbers. A month may enter the comparison only if three things hold. It is the same entity and period the plan claims. Its source files still hash to what the run log recorded. And its EBITDA recomputes to the same figure. Fail one, and the run is rejected — not flagged.

show.event: 'Scope matches' layer slides in
'Hashes match' stacks on
'EBITDA recomputes' lands in terracotta — the accent layer
caption underlines the hard word: rejected

props.sparkLine: Three things, or it is out.

layers.title: Scope matches
layers.sub: same entity and period the plan claims — checked row by row

layers.title: Hashes match
layers.sub: every source file still hashes to what the run log recorded

layers.title: EBITDA recomputes
layers.sub: recalculated from source, then cross-checked against the logged figure

props.caption: Fail any one and the run is rejected — not flagged. Rejected.

beats.narration_text: And this is the actual output. Actual EBITDA: two hundred sixty-one thousand in January, two hundred thirty in February, two hundred sixty-five in March. A thirty-one thousand deterioration, then a thirty-five thousand improvement. Notice the movement column. It says deteriorated and improved. It never says why, and it never says what comes next.

show.event: header and the January row write on
February lands — actual drops to 230000, movement reads DETERIORATED
March lands — 265000, movement reads IMPROVED
the movement column holds: two words, no explanation

props.artifactHeading: Northstar Software Sample · three verified periods
artifactLines: period    budget       actual      variance    change      movement

beats.narration_text: Now the test that actually matters. A detector that flags everything is worthless. So look at payroll. Revenue, cost of goods, and operating expenses are adverse in all three months, and the engine marks them recurring. Payroll is favourable in every period — and the same detector returns no. It discriminates. It does not decorate.

show.event: revenue row writes on — adverse in all three, recurring YES
cogs and opex land, both YES
payroll lands — positive figures across all three periods
the recurring column holds: YES, YES, YES, NO

props.artifactTitle: Category pattern — does it flag everything?
props.artifactHeading: Three categories recur. One does not. That is the control.

beats.narration_text: And then the line I care most about. The report states what it computed. It states that recurrence is a mathematical pattern, not a causal explanation. And the current explanation field ships intentionally blank, with a named owner. The system is allowed to find the pattern. It is not allowed to say why.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. The multi-month trend investigation compares three verified months of synthetic finance data, and reports actual EBITDA moving from two hundred sixty-one thousand, to two hundred thirty, to two hundred sixty-five thousand. It identifies revenue, cost of goods, and operating expenses as recurring adverse categories, and clears payroll — which is how you know the detector discriminates. Every figure is re-derived from source files whose hashes are re-checked at read time, behind fifteen refusal paths. It supplies no forecast, no recommendation, and no cause. Forty-nine tests pass. The recipe still says draft, and the human gate is still open.

props.artifactHeading: A comparison engine that refuses fifteen ways
artifactLines: Compares three verified months: actual EBITDA 261,000 → 230,000 → 265,000.
Flags revenue, COGS and opex as recurring adverse — and clears payroll, so it discriminates.
Every figure re-derived from source; hashes re-checked at read time; 15 refusal paths guard entry.
Supplies no forecast, no recommendation, and no cause — recurrence is a pattern, not an explanation.
49 tests pass. Recipe still DRAFT, materiality unapproved, human gate OPEN.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take a report my system generates and list every number on it. For each one, tell me what would have to be true for that number to be wrong, and whether my code currently checks it. Then tell me which checks I am missing. Run that against something you have built. The uncomfortable part is the last question — most pipelines verify their inputs once, at the start, and then trust every number derived from them forever.
